definition: In Norse mythology, the primordial realm of mist, cold, and darkness, one of the two forces that shaped the world at creation.
origin: From Old Norse Niflheimr, a compound of nifl (mist, fog) + heimr (home, world). Existing before the world itself, Niflheim's icy rivers met the fire of Muspelheim across the void of Ginnungagap, and the meltwater of that collision gave rise to the giant Ymir.

definition: In Norse mythology, the primordial realm of fire, one of the two forces that shaped the world at creation, home to the fire giant Surtr.
origin: From Old Norse Muspellsheimr, combining an obscure element muspell (of uncertain meaning, possibly "world-destroyer") with heimr (home, world). Its searing heat met the ice of Niflheim across Ginnungagap to spark creation, and at Ragnarok its guardian Surtr is prophesied to march out and set the nine worlds ablaze.

origin: From Old English Wodnesdaeg (Woden's day), naming the day for Woden, the Anglo-Saxon form of the god Odin. The Germanic peoples renamed the Roman day of Mercury, dies Mercurii, after their own god of wisdom and war, since Woden and Mercury were seen as parallel figures.

definition: The sixth day of the week, following Thursday and preceding Saturday.
origin: From Old English Frigedaeg (Frigg's day), replacing the Roman dies Veneris, day of Venus, with a Germanic goddess of love and marriage.
